edits.english: GEMARA: Rav Taḥlifa bar Avdimi says that Shmuel says: With regard to Christians, according to the statement of Rabbi Yishmael, it is always prohibited to engage in business with them. Since their festival, Sunday, occurs every week, and the three days before and after it are prohibited, one cannot engage in business with them on any day of the week.

לעולם אסור - שלשה לפניו ושלשה לאחריו והוא עצמו, כלומר: כל שבעת ימי השבת:

edits.english: It is always prohibited: [This means] three days before Sunday and three days after it, as well as the day itself; that is to say, all seven days of the week.

The mishna teaches: And the Rabbis say: It is prohibited to engage in business with gentiles before their festivals, but it is permitted to do so after their festivals. The Gemara asks: The statement of these Rabbis is identical to that of the first tanna in the mishna on 2a! The Gemara answers: The question of whether the three days include the days of the festivals themselves or whether they refer to the three days without the festivals is the difference between them. The first tanna holds that the prohibition applies to the three days without the festivals, and the Rabbis in this mishna hold that it applies to the days of the festivals themselves and the days preceding them, totaling three days.

edits.hebrew: תנא קמא סבר הן בלא אידיהן - כדדייקינן לעיל: דקתני "לפני אידיהן של עובדי כוכבים שלשה ימים", שמע מינה: שלשה לפניהם לבד האיד קאמר:

edits.english: The first tanna holds [it means] the days without the festival: As we inferred above from the fact that the first mishna teaches: 'Before the festivals of gentiles three days'. Conclude from it that he meant three days before them, besides the festival.

edits.hebrew: ורבנן בתראי - דלא יהבו סימנא, איכא למימר: הואיל ולא אשכחן מידי ביניהן, איכא למימר בהא אתו לאפלוגי: דהן ואידיהן שלשה קאמר:

edits.english: And the later Rabbis: Since they did not give an indicator, it can be said that since we do not find anything else between the two mishnayot, they must come to disagree about this: That the festival and the preceding days together are three.

If you wish, say instead that the status of profits earned from engaging in business with a gentile is the difference between them. The first tanna holds that if one violated the prohibition and engaged in business with a gentile, the profit is permitted, and the Rabbis in this mishna hold that if one engaged in business with a gentile, the profit is prohibited.

edits.hebrew: רבנן בתראי סברי נשא ונתן אסור - סתמא קאמרינן, ולא קתני "אסור לשאת ולתת" כתנא קמא, דמשמע: לכתחלה הוא דלא, הא דיעבד שפיר דמי:

edits.english: The later Rabbis hold [if] one engaged in business it is prohibited: They state the law plainly, and it does not teach 'it is prohibited to engage in business' as the first tanna did, which would imply that the prohibition is only ab initio but that after the fact it is permitted.

And if you wish, say instead that the ruling of Shmuel is the difference between them. As Shmuel says: In the Diaspora, it is prohibited to engage in business with gentiles only on the day of their festival itself. The first tanna accepts the statement of Shmuel, but the Rabbis in this mishna do not accept the statement of Shmuel.

edits.hebrew: בגולה - אין העובדי כוכבים אדוקין כל כך בעבודת כוכבים, כדאמרינן לקמן: "עובדי כוכבים שבחוצה לארץ לאו עובדי עבודת כוכבים נינהו וכולי". ועוד: דמסתפינן מינייהו:

edits.english: In the Diaspora: The gentiles are not so devoted to idol worship, as we say later: 'Gentiles outside the Land of Israel are not [truly] idol worshippers, etc.' Moreover, we are afraid of them.

edits.hebrew: רבנן בתראי לית להו דשמואל - דכיון דלא מסיים בהדיא במאי פליגי, איכא למימר: לטפויי אתו, דשמעינן לתנא קמא דקאמר: "לפני אידיהן אסור לשאת ולתת עמהם", וסתמא דמילתא - כשאין יד עובדי כוכבים תקיפה על ישראל קא אמר; ואתו אינהו למימר: לפני אידיהן לעולם אסורין. ואיפכא ליכא לשנויי, דתתריץ שפיר: דסתם תנא בתרא לטפויי אתא:

edits.english: The later Rabbis do not hold like Shmuel: Since it is not explicitly stated in what way they disagree, one can say they came to add a stringency. We heard the first tanna say: 'before their festivals it is prohibited to engage in business with them', and the plain meaning is that he spoke only when the gentiles do not have the upper hand over Israel. These [later Rabbis] then came to say: 'before their festivals it is always prohibited'. The opposite cannot be suggested, as the explanation is settled well only if a later unattributed tanna is assumed to come to add a stringency.

And if you wish, say instead that the ruling of Naḥum the Mede is the difference between them. As it is taught in a baraita that Naḥum the Mede says: It is prohibited to engage in business with gentiles only one day before their festival. The first tanna does not accept the statement of Naḥum the Mede, but the Rabbis in this mishna accept the statement of Naḥum the Mede.

edits.hebrew: רבנן בתראי אית להו כנחום - דלא יהבי חושבנא, אלא "אסור" סתמא קאמרי:

edits.english: The later Rabbis hold like Naḥum: Since they did not specify a count of days, but rather said 'prohibited' in a general sense.

The Gemara returns to discuss the matter itself. Naḥum the Mede says: It is prohibited to engage in business with gentiles only one day before their festival. The other Sages said to him: This matter should be lost and not stated, as it is not the halakha. The Gemara asks: But aren’t there the Rabbis in this mishna, who hold in accordance with his opinion? The Gemara answers: Who are the Rabbis mentioned there? It is Naḥum the Mede himself.

edits.hebrew: נשתקע הדבר - לא יצא דבר זה מפי אדם לעולם. לשון אחר: לא יצא דבר זה לחוץ:

edits.english: The matter should be lost: This statement should never have been uttered by anyone. Another explanation: This matter should not have been publicized.
